div.ab:
If there were an ear that would hearken lovingly, gladly now would I speak plainly; but if love listen not to me, why should I discourse? For without love my word is stripped of profit. The love of virtue is grown tasteless to men; neither is instruction desired when it is set forth. Little by little the world has left goodly customs, and has put away from it hope and love and faith. The fear of the Lord is the cause of all good: to-day it is little esteemed, and therefore have offerings ceased. Evil has prevailed and crept upon men;
and it gives not place for the performance of good. Not almsgiving alone have men left to-day, but the oblations also of their departed they have withheld: They have ceased from all vows and oblations and tithes. This has come to men, and they give no heed to it.

This sacrifice was left to the world to be sanctified withal; and men have now left it, and honour it not duly. In the bread and
wine, which is a mystery of the Body and the Blood, all sacrifices are spiritually summed up; and by it both they that were before were brought near to God, and for them also that are come after there comes a pardoning from the Majesty. With bread and wine Melchizedek, the high priest, entered in to minister before God mystically. With this sacrifice, wherein is neither stench nor smoke, he was ministering as priest, that he might depict a type of the things to come. He who in his fulfilment was made a priest for ever chose to offer bread and wine rather than all sacrifices. He knew before, as a spiritual man who judges all things, that save by this the whole world is not pardoned.
Whereas he had the pattern and the examples of Noah and Abel, he liked not to bring in the blood of animals before God. Spiritually he was stirred and moved in his soul, and he understood that bread and wine alone were fitting to offer. These mysteries by which the Church abides to-day, the same did Melchizedek employ, lo, from of old. Moses also, the great prophet, who offered up sacrifices, hinted how goodly is this pure sacrifice. With the shewbread that departed not from the table,—with this did he enhance all his sacrifices mystically. Albeit they were sheep and oxen that he was offering, yet the bread he honoured more than all by its abiding. Before the face of the Lord he set it upon the table, and bread of the face he called it—he the great prophet. With this bread did he enhance all sacrifices; for a great mystery of the holy Body in it shone forth. And if the former men carried it with pomp upon their hands, how much more should the latter men apply themselves to it. And if the Old Testament set store by it, that itself by it might be honoured,
how much more should the New be instant in its honour. And if when it was but bread it was more honoured than all sacrifices: now that it is the Body, what sacrifice is there so great? For the former men did but shew forth types by their oblations, and gave to the latter men a goodly pattern of the realities.

But the King's Daughter took not the similitudes from the Old; neither for this cause does she break the bread of the Mysteries to-day. In the upper chamber she saw her Lord break His Body; and from Him she learned to do daily as He appointed to her. It was not Melchizedek taught the Church how she should do this: on her Lord she gazed, and as He did so does she daily. Not from Moses, who was a man, did she receive the type; but Jesus, who was God, taught her the Mystery. And lo, she is careful of it, and bears it in triumph, and glories in it; for it is the great sacrifice whereby the living and the dead are made perfect.

And wherefore to-day is this good, so exceeding great, by many lightly esteemed and not performed? Men have despised the bread of the sacrament, and bring it not: and what shall I speak, or why, or how, or to whom?
Shall I be altogether silent from reproof with the discerning? or shall I speak lovingly with them that have knowledge? O thou that hearkenest to me with love, to Thee will I speak: with love receive, for it is love that moves me also to speak. Let not the Lord's bread depart for thee from His table; and with the wine of His sacrament daily make libation spiritually. Bring bread and wine and love to the place of atonement, that with thy memorial the priest may enter in before the Majesty. On the stones of the ephod Moses wrote the names of the tribes, that the priest might bring in the memorials of them to the holy of holies. And thou, on the eucharistic bread (perîstâ) inscribe thy memorial and that of thy departed ones, and give it to the priest to offer before God. Make a supper, and call thy dead that they come to the sacrifice, which is the harbour and rest of all spirits. Thou that lovest the dead man, by this show thy love for him: not with making of a great lamentation that profits him not. Give to God his name and his memorial with thy oblation; and thy faith shall not be disappointed of that which is
just. Set his memorial upon the table of the house of atonement, with the bread and wine which is a mystery of the Body and the Blood.

To the women's side will I now speak severally,
if they will listen to me with the ears of the soul lovingly. To the dead in the tombs, lo, they go about to weep, and with wailings they shew their love for their departed ones. They have left the church and its service and its offerings, and are gone to weep for their dear ones among the tombs. O thou believing woman, seek thy beloved in the holy temple with God, in whose hands lie all the spirits. Call not to the dead in the grave, for he heareth thee not. He is not there: seek for him here in the house of atonement. Hither all the souls of all the departed assemble; for this place is a harbour of life to them that recline therein. Here are set forth their memorials and their names in the great book of the Godhead, wherein is every one of them. The blood of the cross has sprinkled a quickening upon the souls; and its mighty power has drawn them to come unto it. And since thy departed, O woman, is surely here, why goest thou about among the tombs, as one of the foolish? Is thy gift lightly valued, or is thy faith not perfect? It is custom that has drawn thee after these follies
, and forcibly carried thee off to the tombs to speak with thy departed; and thou hast many times stumbled in thy haste without heeding. If there were any love of God in thy soul, instead of wailing prayer would be begotten in thy mouth. Cease, wretched woman, from this ignorant notion; and rest thy soul on the understanding of faith. Let thy love for thy dear one resemble love; and with oblations and prayers make his memorial. Thy dead is not profited by thy weeping at the grave; but thine oblation greatly benefits both thee and thy dead. Those tears that were shed upon the grave, sprinkle them here in the church wisely.

That the dead are profited by the oblations which the
living make, appears to me to need no questioning; but if a man will dare to make question of things manifest, he may easily hear the truth of doctrine. Judas Maccabaeus, that righteous army-leader, took thought and offered up a sacrifice for the dead; and the man's great faith had its due effect. His victory itself bore witness to his sacrifices, how profitable they were. That the dead were profited by the oblation of that illustrious man, his contest with the Greeks manifestly proclaims. He was a wise man and a mighty warrior of God, great in faith and knowledge and full of zeal: and for the dead he performed sacrifices and made atonement for them, that the world might learn his deed of love and imitate him. And if while Death was alive and ruling and wearing the crown, sacrifices were able to make atonement for the dead under his dominion: now that he is slain and his place uprooted and his crown taken away, who will henceforth doubt concerning atonement for the dead? Judas offered the blood of animals to the Lord
and reconciled Him to the dead, and made atonement for them that were defiled: the Church to-day with no perishable sacrifices makes atonement for the dead, but with the blood of the Immortal. And if that common sacrifice of Judas made atonement, how much more rather shall that great slaying of the Son of God cleanse all.

On behalf of the souls of the dead the priest enters in and stands and sets the bread and wine of the sacrament upon the table; and the death of Jesus he commemorates there, likewise his resurrection. And every one that is departed he calls to the sacrifice to be pardoned; and all who have offered and brought the eucharistic bread (perîstâ) he commemorates with love. And for a memorial
of their departed he signs the Mystery; and on behalf of all the dead who have fallen asleep he offers up the sacrifices. He calls to the Father and reminds Him of the death of His Son; and the Spirit sets forth and comes down and dwells on the oblation; and He becomes corporate in it with mighty power, and it becomes the Body; and by His brooding He makes the mingled wine the Blood. And forthwith the sacrifice is the Body and Blood which sanctifies all. By this sacrifice the priest makes atonement for all the dead; for in it there is power to conquer Death and lay waste his place.
To the odour of life which comes forth from the great sacrifice all the souls assemble and come to be pardoned; and through the quickening which the Body of the Son of God imparts, daily the dead scent the odour of life, and by it (sc. the Body) they are pardoned. Wherefore be careful of the memorial of your beloved ones, and of the oblation which is able to pardon your departed.

But if there be one who says that the departed is not pardoned by the oblation which the living makes, and is not profited by it, saying on this wise: Others have made it, while he perceives it not: what does it avail him? A man by his own works is profited, not by those of his fellows. The merit of the living man is increased by his oblation: for he makes it, and he is profited by it, and not others. For the oblation that the living makes for the departed, without himself how can he profit by it? How can one man's righteousness
affect that of another? He has offered and brought it, and he is benefited, not the departed.—Against him who says these things I say, that the Church is wont to pardon even him who is unconscious. The child who is baptized while he is unconscious of the baptism:
has he received his own, or not perchance, as thou sayest? The Church pardons them that are not conscious and them that are conscious: for faith without doubt raises up the dead. She receives the child of a few days old from his parents, and baptizes and pardons and sanctifies him, while he perceives it not. If the Sacrament pardon not the dead, as thou sayest, neither does baptism avail the child who is unconscious of it. And hence are all the mysteries of the Church void; and in vain does she toil for the departed to pardon them. Why does the priest say: Pray ye over every one that is departed? And why does he baptize the child who perceives it not, and sanctify him? The believing parents bring the child to baptism; and the Lord sees their faith, and sanctifies him, and admits him to the adoption of sons, while he knows it not, and writes his name in the Church of the first-born, and he perceives it not. So also believing heirs of a dead man departed bring bread and wine in his name to the holy altar; and prayer of priest and people is made over the departed; and the Lord pardons the dead man whose commemoration they are making. But if the dead is not pardoned by means of the oblation, neither has the child in baptism entered among the sons.
If the offering of the living profits the living only: the parents who have offered and caused the child to be baptized,—it is they that are profited. Where then is the faith that quickens the dead, and makes prayer for the departed to pardon them, and brings down children to the font to sanctify them, and has the hope that nothing she asks will be denied her? Sure is the hope of the King's Bride, and it is not disappointed; and comely and great and blameless is her faith. With the glorious Mysteries she ministers to her Lord spiritually, and at her service the watchers are in holy awe. The faith of the Church is this, good friends, that she is able to make the bread and wine the Body and the Blood. She breaks the bread, and she knows it not for bread, but the Body; and she mingles the wine, and affirms that it is Blood in her vessel. And she reads the names of all her dead over the oblation, and she mingles them with her in the spiritual sacri-
fices. And she assembles them to the supper of the Body and the Blood, and they banquet with her spiritually at her board.

O good friends, ye that know the mysteries of faith, without doubting make the oblations for your departed. The customs which the Church has taught her sons, why are they fallen out, and to many are grown tasteless, and are lightly esteemed, and are not observed?
Despised and dishonoured and meanly the loaf (qesâthâ) is brought to the house of God to be offered. There are many who have altogether made an end, and bring it not; and there is that when he brings it, brings it not himself in person: by the hands of his maid servant he sends the sacrifice to the house of God. And as though it were a dishonour to him to bring in his own hands his sacrifice to the Lord, the despised dependents of his house, who are set to the meanest works, them he commands to bring his sacrifice, while he is absent. Why, good sir, dost thou not bring thy sacrifice in thine own hands, like Abraham, who carried the calf to the angels? He and his consort made them ready and stood to minister, and performed not that which was due by the hands of others. To-day the faith of men is waxed little, and love is grown lukewarm, and the sense of things seemly is lacking. What rich man is there that has brought the eucharistic loaf (qesâthâ) to the house of God, and carried it in his hands when he brings it in to the house of atonement? Either he brings it not at all or, if he brings it, he does but command the menials of his house to bring his sacrifice, while he is not present. Blessed is the widow who bears her sacrifice in her hands,
and the bereaved who carries it and glories in it. She sends not the loaf (qesâthâ) to the Lord, like the rich man: she herself offers it, and cries out earnestly that He will accept it of her. She, like the priest, brings in her vow to God, earnestly making mention of her dead over her oblation. Such a one has known how to offer and bring sacrifices to the Lord: not the rich man, who sends it as though to one in need. Acceptable is the oblation of the bereaved woman when it is offered, and with it mingled tears and love and faith: the loaf in her hands, and tears in her eyes, and praise in her mouth: and as her oblation great also is the offering of her faith; for save with love the oblation is not accepted.
Blessed is He who in His love has sacrificed His Only-begotten for many.

noteGrp.note: n. 3 There would appear to be a verse wanting here.
n. 4 R reads to be pardoned.
n. 5 R bring; which is perhaps the better reading.
n. 6 R a spiritual type.
n. 7 I.e. Christ.
n. 8 1 Cor. ii 15.
n. 9 Lit. bread of the face.
n. 10 So Bedjan's text, I do not know on what authority. R reads with their sacrifices; P celebrated it above their sacrifices. The last reading is most in keeping with the context.
n. 11 Sc. the Church.
n. 12 Or holy bread.

n. 13 This may merely mean the church, or the sanctuary; but it possibly denotes a special chapel where Masses for the dead were celebrated. The expression is used several times in this Homily to describe the place to which the offerings of bread and wine are to be brought.

n. 14 This is a well-established term for the bread used in the sacrifice of the Mass. Cf. Acts ii 46, where in the Syriac version it translates the Greek word arton, the bread which the Apostles were breaking from house to house.
n. 15 The writer is perhaps thinking of the women's part of the church.
n. 16 R and thou hast multiplied words.
n. 17 Cf. Gen. xv 9.
n. 18 Lit. fragment, morsel: another technical term for the eucharistic bread, and synonymous with pĕrîstâ.
n. 19 2 Macc. xii 43 ff.
n. 20 Lit. wrought its own.

n. 21 Narsai also makes the setting of the bread and wine on the altar symbolize our Lord's death and burial, and the consecration His resurrection: cf. Texts and Studies, VIII no. 1 p. 21: As soon as the bread and wine are set upon the altar they shew forth a symbol of the death of the Son, also of His resurrection; wherefore that Spirit which raised Him from the dead comes down now and celebrates the Mysteries of the resurrection of His Body (see also pp. 3, 4, 23, 24, 30).

n. 22 Compare the prayer of Intercession in the Liturgies of St Mark (Brightman, Liturgies Eastern and Western, vol. 1 p. 129 ll. 20-30), the Greek St James (Br. p. 56 ll. 16-19), and Syriac St James (Br. p. 91 ll. 26-34).
n. 23 R sacrifice.

n. 24 This is the reading of the Roman MS (R). P has and the Mystery becomes corporate by Him in the bread. But this is awkward, and indeed hardly possible. If however we supply a single letter, we get the same sense as that in the text: and He becomes corporate in the bread of the Mystery. If such language appears startling, it is nevertheless to be met with elsewhere in early Syriac writers (see Texts and Studies, vol. VIII no. 1 pp. 147-149). But there is no reason to suppose that it implies a habit among the Syrians of regarding the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Blessed Trinity, as the content of the Eucharist: it is probably only a relic of an earlier and inaccurate Syriac terminology, in which the Holy Spirit, or the Spirit of Christ, was sometimes used to denote the second Divine Person, especially as the divine nature of our Lord (for examples of such usage see the sixth Homily of Aphraates passim). It may be remarked that the Syriac verb translated becomes corporate is often employed to express the incarnation of God the Word: thus in the Nestorian Creed it stands for incarnatus est.
n. 25 I.e. without himself (the departed) being the offerer.
n. 26 I.e. has he himself received the effect of his baptism?
n. 27 I.e. angels
n. 28 So R: P and discernment and faith are lacking.
n. 29 R with, which seems better.
